claim: Cerox1 is a 1.2 kb, two exon, intergenic transcript in mouse.
source: Mouse Cerox1 is a 1.2 kb, two exon, intergenic transcript which shares a bidirectional promoter with the SRY (sex determining region Y)-box 8 (Sox8) gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the structural characteristics of mouse Cerox1.

claim: Mouse Cerox1 shares a bidirectional promoter with the Sox8 gene.
source: Mouse Cerox1 is a 1.2 kb, two exon, intergenic transcript which shares a bidirectional promoter with the SRY (sex determining region Y)-box 8 (Sox8) gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this relationship and references Figure 1A showing the genomic locus.

claim: A human orthologous transcript to mouse Cerox1 was identified by sequence similarity and conserved synteny.
source: A human orthologous transcript (CEROX1, GenBank Accession BC098409) was identified by sequence similarity and conserved synteny (60–70% nucleotide identity within alignable regions, Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the identification method and provides sequence identity data.

claim: Human CEROX1 and mouse Cerox1 share 60-70% nucleotide identity within alignable regions.
source: A human orthologous transcript (CEROX1, GenBank Accession BC098409) was identified by sequence similarity and conserved synteny (60–70% nucleotide identity within alignable regions, Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific sequence identity percentages.

claim: Both mouse Cerox1 and human CEROX1 have low protein coding potential.
source: Both mouse and human transcripts have low protein coding potential (Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and no evidence for translation from available proteomic datasets.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references computational analysis and proteomic data.

claim: There is no evidence for translation of Cerox1/CEROX1 from available proteomic datasets.
source: Both mouse and human transcripts have low protein coding potential (Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and no evidence for translation from available proteomic datasets.
evidence: The manuscript states the absence of proteomic evidence for translation.

claim: The CEROX1 promoter shows greater sequence conservation than the adjacent SOX8 promoter.
source: The genomic evolutionary rate profiling (GERP) score indicates a higher extent of conservation of the CEROX1 promoter (shaded pink) than the adjacent SOX8 promoter (shaded green).
evidence: The manuscript references GERP scores shown in Figure 1B indicating differential conservation.

claim: Cerox1 expression levels are within the top 13% of a set of 879 lncRNAs with associated CAGE clusters.
source: Second, from expression data, its levels in primary tissues and cells are exceptionally high, within the top 13% of a set of 879 lncRNAs with associated cap analysis of gene expression (CAGE) clusters (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific ranking data from CAGE expression analysis.

claim: Cerox1 expression is particularly high in neuroglia, neural progenitor cells and oligodendrocyte progenitors.
source: Expression is particularly high in neuroglia, neural progenitor cells and oligodendrocyte progenitors (Bergmann et al., 2015; Mercer et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies and references supplementary figure showing expression patterns.

claim: Cerox1 is notable in its higher expression in the adult brain than 64% of all protein coding genes.
source: Cerox1 is notable in its higher expression in the adult brain than 64% of all protein coding genes.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific comparison to protein-coding gene expression.

claim: Cerox1 expression is developmentally regulated.
source: Cerox1 expression is also developmentally regulated. For example, it is a known marker gene for type one pre-haematopoietic stem cells in the dorsal aorta (Zhou et al., 2016) and its expression is high in mouse embryos beyond the 21 somite stage (https://dmdd.org.uk/).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work and developmental database showing developmental expression patterns.

claim: Cerox1 is a known marker gene for type one pre-haematopoietic stem cells in the dorsal aorta.
source: For example, it is a known marker gene for type one pre-haematopoietic stem cells in the dorsal aorta (Zhou et al., 2016) and its expression is high in mouse embryos beyond the 21 somite stage (https://dmdd.org.uk/).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study identifying Cerox1 as a marker gene.

claim: Single nucleotide variants are significantly associated with CEROX1 expression and anthropomorphic traits measured in the UK Biobank.
source: Third, single nucleotide variants are significantly associated both with CEROX1 expression and anthropomorphic traits, measured in the UK Biobank.
evidence: The manuscript describes genetic association analysis results from UK Biobank data.

claim: rs3809674 is significantly associated with standing and sitting heights, arm fat-free mass, arm predicted mass, trunk fat-free or predicted mass, and whole body fat-free mass.
source: For example, rs3809674 is significantly associated with standing and sitting heights; arm fat-free mass (left or right); arm predicted mass (left or right); trunk fat-free or predicted mass; and whole body fat-free mass (p<5×10−8, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific p-values for genetic associations with anthropomorphic traits.

claim: rs3809674 is a CEROX1 expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) for 30 GTEx tissues.
source: this variant is also a CEROX1 expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) for 30 GTEx tissues (p≤0.05), some with absolute normalised effect sizes reaching 0.83 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports eQTL analysis results from GTEx data.

claim: rs3809674 has a minor allele frequency of 28% in 1000 Genomes data.
source: These variations affect a large fraction of the human population (minor allele frequency of 28% in 1000 Genomes data).
evidence: The manuscript provides allele frequency data from the 1000 Genomes project.

claim: Cerox1 depletion may impair the contributions of stem cell or B cell differentiation to haematopoiesis in a mouse model.
source: Finally, it has recently been demonstrated in a mouse model of haematopoietic lineage differentiation that Cerox1 depletion may impair the contributions of stem cell or B cell differentiation to haematopoiesis (Delás et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study demonstrating this functional role.

claim: In mouse N2A cells, Cerox1 is enriched in the cytoplasmic fraction.
source: In mouse neuroblastoma (N2A) cells the most highly expressed Cerox1 transcript (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G) is enriched in the cytoplasmic fraction (Figure 1F)
evidence: The manuscript reports cell fractionation results showing cytoplasmic localization.

claim: Mouse Cerox1 is 15-fold enriched in the cytoplasm of N2A cells.
source: By fractionation, mouse Cerox1 is 15-fold enriched in the cytoplasm of N2A cells (n = 5; error bars s.e.m.).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative fractionation data with sample size.

claim: Mouse Cerox1 has a short half-life of 36 ± 16 mins in N2A cells.
source: In mouse neuroblastoma (N2A) cells the most highly expressed Cerox1 transcript (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G) is enriched in the cytoplasmic fraction (Figure 1F) with a short half-life of 36 ± 16 mins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: The manuscript reports transcript stability measurements using actinomycin D treatment.

claim: Cerox1 is mainly associated with the ribosome-free fraction in N2A cells.
source: In mouse neuroblastoma (N2A) cells the most highly expressed Cerox1 transcript (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G) is enriched in the cytoplasmic fraction (Figure 1F) with a short half-life of 36 ± 16 mins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) and is mainly associated with the ribosome-free fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The manuscript reports sucrose gradient fractionation results.

claim: Cerox1 overexpression led to differential expression of 286 distal genes.
source: In contrast, Cerox1 overexpression led to differential expression of 286 distal genes (q < 0.05, Bonferroni multiple testing correction; Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The manuscript reports microarray analysis results with statistical correction.

claim: 83% of genes differentially expressed after Cerox1 overexpression were upregulated.
source: In contrast, Cerox1 overexpression led to differential expression of 286 distal genes (q < 0.05, Bonferroni multiple testing correction; Supplementary file 2), of which an unexpected and large majority (83%; 237) were upregulated (p<10−6; binomial test).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and statistical significance from microarray data.

claim: There is considerable (≥20 fold) enrichment of the mitochondrial respiratory chain gene ontology term among upregulated genes after Cerox1 overexpression.
source: Our attention was immediately drawn to the considerable (≥20 fold) enrichment of the mitochondrial respiratory chain gene ontology term among upregulated genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports gene ontology enrichment analysis results.

claim: Of 15 oxidative phosphorylation genes whose transcripts were up-regulated following Cerox1 overexpression, 53% were subunits of Complex I.
source: Of 15 oxidative phosphorylation genes whose transcripts were up-regulated following Cerox1 overexpression 53% were subunits of Complex I, 13% were subunits of Complex III and 33% were subunits of Complex IV.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of complex subunit representation in Figure 2B.

claim: Twelve of 35 nuclear encoded complex I subunits or assembly factors transcripts increased substantially and significantly (>40%) following Cerox1 overexpression.
source: Twelve of 35 nuclear encoded complex I subunits or assembly factors transcripts increased substantially and significantly (>40%) following Cerox1 overexpression; we consider these to be gene expression biomarkers for Cerox1 activity in the mouse N2A system (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR validation results for complex I subunit transcripts.

claim: In the reciprocal Cerox1 knock-down experiment using sh92, all 12 complex I biomarker transcripts were reduced in abundance, three significantly.
source: In the reciprocal Cerox1 knock-down experiment, all 12 were reduced in abundance using sh92, three significantly, with a concordant pattern observed for the less effective shRNA, sh1159 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR results from knockdown experiments.

claim: Western blots showed approximately 2.0-fold protein level increases for NDUFS1 and NDUFS3 following Cerox1 overexpression.
source: Western blots using reliable antibodies for the key complex I catalytic core proteins NDUFS1 and NDUFS3 showed approximately 2.0-fold protein level increases that surpassed their ~ 1.4 fold transcript level changes (median 2.4 and 1.4-fold increases [p=0.0013 and 0.002], respectively; Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative western blot results with statistical significance.

claim: The protein level increases for NDUFS1 and NDUFS3 surpassed their transcript level changes following Cerox1 overexpression.
source: Western blots using reliable antibodies for the key complex I catalytic core proteins NDUFS1 and NDUFS3 showed approximately 2.0-fold protein level increases that surpassed their ~ 1.4 fold transcript level changes (median 2.4 and 1.4-fold increases [p=0.0013 and 0.002], respectively; Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript compares protein and transcript level changes showing amplification at the protein level.

claim: Ten metabolites are significantly different in N2A cells overexpressing Cerox1.
source: Ten metabolites are significantly different in N2A cells overexpressing Cerox1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports LC-MS metabolomics results.

claim: N2A cells overexpressing Cerox1 show a significant increase in the reduced glutathione to oxidized glutathione ratio (GSH:GSSG).
source: These cells show a significant increase in the reduced glutathione to oxidized glutathione ratio (GSH:GSSG, p=1.3×10−3, Figure 2D Inset) indicative of a more favourable cellular redox state.
evidence: The manuscript reports metabolite ratio measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1-overexpressing cells exhibited a 43% reduction in cell cycle activity.
source: Cerox1-overexpressing cells also exhibited a 43% reduction in cell cycle activity, yet without a change in the proportion of live/dead cells or a deviation from normal cell cycle proportions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I,J,K).
evidence: The manuscript reports cell counting and viability assay results.

claim: Complex I enzymatic activity increased by 22% after Cerox1 overexpression in N2A cells.
source: Indeed, complex I and complex IV enzymatic activities increased substantially after Cerox1 overexpression (by 22%, p=0.01; by 50%, p=0.003, respectively; 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results with statistical significance.

claim: Complex IV enzymatic activity increased by 50% after Cerox1 overexpression in N2A cells.
source: Indeed, complex I and complex IV enzymatic activities increased substantially after Cerox1 overexpression (by 22%, p=0.01; by 50%, p=0.003, respectively; 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1 overexpression resulted in an 85% increase in overall basal oxygen consumption in N2A cells.
source: These complexes' more rapid catalytic rates resulted, unexpectedly, in large increases in: (i) overall basal oxygen consumption (by 85%), (ii) ATP-linked oxygen consumption (by 107%) and, (iii) maximum uncoupled respiration (by 59%; p=5×10−4, p=1×10−4, p=4×10−3, respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1 overexpression resulted in a 107% increase in ATP-linked oxygen consumption in N2A cells.
source: These complexes' more rapid catalytic rates resulted, unexpectedly, in large increases in: (i) overall basal oxygen consumption (by 85%), (ii) ATP-linked oxygen consumption (by 107%) and, (iii) maximum uncoupled respiration (by 59%; p=5×10−4, p=1×10−4, p=4×10−3, respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1 overexpression resulted in a 59% increase in maximum uncoupled respiration in N2A cells.
source: These complexes' more rapid catalytic rates resulted, unexpectedly, in large increases in: (i) overall basal oxygen consumption (by 85%), (ii) ATP-linked oxygen consumption (by 107%) and, (iii) maximum uncoupled respiration (by 59%; p=5×10−4, p=1×10−4, p=4×10−3, respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements with statistical significance.

claim: After sh92-mediated Cerox1 knockdown, complex I enzymatic activity decreased by 11%.
source: Conversely, after sh92-mediated Cerox1 knockdown complex I and complex IV enzymatic activities decreased significantly (by 11%, p=0.03% and 19%, p=0.02, respectively; Figure 3C)
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results from knockdown experiments with statistical significance.

claim: After sh92-mediated Cerox1 knockdown, complex IV enzymatic activity decreased by 19%.
source: Conversely, after sh92-mediated Cerox1 knockdown complex I and complex IV enzymatic activities decreased significantly (by 11%, p=0.03% and 19%, p=0.02, respectively; Figure 3C)
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results from knockdown experiments with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1 knockdown resulted in a 53% decrease in basal oxygen consumption.
source: with concomitant large decreases in basal oxygen consumption (53%), ATP linked oxygen consumption (52%) and maximal uncoupled respiration (61%; p=0.011, p=0.034, p=0.042 respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse measurements from knockdown experiments with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1 knockdown resulted in a 52% decrease in ATP linked oxygen consumption.
source: with concomitant large decreases in basal oxygen consumption (53%), ATP linked oxygen consumption (52%) and maximal uncoupled respiration (61%; p=0.011, p=0.034, p=0.042 respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse measurements from knockdown experiments with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1 knockdown resulted in a 61% decrease in maximal uncoupled respiration.
source: with concomitant large decreases in basal oxygen consumption (53%), ATP linked oxygen consumption (52%) and maximal uncoupled respiration (61%; p=0.011, p=0.034, p=0.042 respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse measurements from knockdown experiments with statistical significance.

claim: The enzymatic activities of complexes II, III and citrate synthase remained unaltered by changes in Cerox1 levels.
source: These observed changes in enzymatic activity were not due to changes in mitochondria number because the enzymatic activities of complexes II, III and citrate synthase (Figure 3A,B), and the mitochondrial-to-nuclear genome ratio (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), each remained unaltered by changes in Cerox1 levels.
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity measurements showing no change for these complexes.

claim: The mitochondrial-to-nuclear genome ratio remained unaltered by changes in Cerox1 levels.
source: These observed changes in enzymatic activity were not due to changes in mitochondria number because the enzymatic activities of complexes II, III and citrate synthase (Figure 3A,B), and the mitochondrial-to-nuclear genome ratio (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), each remained unaltered by changes in Cerox1 levels.
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR measurements of mitochondrial and nuclear genome ratios.

claim: In Cerox1 knockdown N2A cells, ROS levels were increased by almost 20%.
source: In Cerox1 knockdown N2A cells ROS levels were increased significantly, by almost 20% (p=4.2×10−6; Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports ROS measurements using Amplex Red assay with statistical significance.

claim: In cells overexpressing Cerox1, ROS production was nearly halved.
source: Conversely, in cells overexpressing Cerox1, ROS production was nearly halved (p=3.5×10−7; Figure 4A)
evidence: The manuscript reports ROS measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Protein carbonylation was reduced by 35% in cells overexpressing Cerox1.
source: Conversely, in cells overexpressing Cerox1, ROS production was nearly halved (p=3.5×10−7; Figure 4A), and protein carbonylation, a measure of ROS-induced damage, was reduced by 35% (p=1×10−3; Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports protein carbonylation measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1 overexpression protects cells against rotenone (complex I inhibitor) by 37%.
source: We next demonstrated that the increased activities of complex I and complex IV induced by Cerox1 protect cells against the deleterious effects of specific mitochondrial complex inhibitors, specifically rotenone and sodium azide (complex I and complex IV inhibitors, 37% and 58% respectively, p<0.01)
evidence: The manuscript reports cell viability assays with inhibitor treatment and statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1 overexpression protects cells against sodium azide (complex IV inhibitor) by 58%.
source: We next demonstrated that the increased activities of complex I and complex IV induced by Cerox1 protect cells against the deleterious effects of specific mitochondrial complex inhibitors, specifically rotenone and sodium azide (complex I and complex IV inhibitors, 37% and 58% respectively, p<0.01)
evidence: The manuscript reports cell viability assays with inhibitor treatment and statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1-knockdown cells were significantly more sensitive to rotenone by 12%.
source: conversely, Cerox1-knockdown cells were significantly more sensitive to rotenone and exposure to heat (12%, p<0.001% and 11%, p<0.01 respectively Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports cell viability assays from knockdown experiments with statistical significance.

claim: Cerox1-knockdown cells were significantly more sensitive to heat exposure by 11%.
source: conversely, Cerox1-knockdown cells were significantly more sensitive to rotenone and exposure to heat (12%, p<0.001% and 11%, p<0.01 respectively Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports cell viability assays from knockdown experiments with statistical significance.

claim: Overexpression of Cerox1 in wildtype mouse embryonic stem cells led to an increase in transcript levels of six complex I subunits.
source: We first tested Cerox1 overexpression in wildtype mouse ES cells and showed that this, again, led to an increase in transcript levels, specifically of six complex I subunits (Figure 5A)
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR results from ES cell experiments.

claim: Overexpression in DicerΔ/Δ cells failed to increase levels of complex I subunit transcripts.
source: In contrast, overexpression in DicerΔ/Δ cells failed to increase levels of these transcripts (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR results from Dicer knockout ES cells.

claim: Cerox1's ability to alter mitochondrial metabolism is miRNA-dependent.
source: These results indicate that Cerox1's ability to alter mitochondrial metabolism is miRNA-dependent.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the Dicer knockout experiment results.

claim: A mutated Cerox1 transcript with five mutated MREs failed to alter complex I transcript levels when overexpressed in mouse N2A cells.
source: All five MREs conserved in mouse Cerox1 and human CEROX1 for N2A-expressed miRNAs (Figure 5B Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) were mutated by inversion of their seed regions. This mutated Cerox1 transcript failed to alter either complex I transcript levels or enzyme activities when overexpressed in mouse N2A cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR and enzyme activity results from experiments with mutated Cerox1.

claim: The 5xMRE mutant Cerox1 failed to alter OXPHOS enzymatic activity compared to the control.
source: All five MREs conserved in mouse Cerox1 and human CEROX1 for N2A-expressed miRNAs (Figure 5B Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) were mutated by inversion of their seed regions. This mutated Cerox1 transcript failed to alter either complex I transcript levels or enzyme activities when overexpressed in mouse N2A cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results with statistical analysis.

claim: Overexpression of miR-488-3p caused the greatest depletion of the Cerox1 transcript (>90% knockdown).
source: Overexpression of the tissue-restricted miRNA miR-488–3p (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C; Landgraf et al., 2007; Isakova and Quake, 2018) caused the greatest depletion of the Cerox1 transcript (Figure 5E)
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR results from miRNA overexpression experiments.

claim: Dual fluorescent RNA in situ hybridization indicates the proximity of miR-488-3p and Cerox1 within the N2A cell.
source: Dual fluorescent RNA in situ hybridization of miR-488–3p and Cerox1 indicates the proximity of these non-coding RNAs within the N2A cell (Figure 5F)
evidence: The manuscript reports fluorescent in situ hybridization imaging results.

claim: Both Cerox1 and miR-488-3p are localised in the cytoplasm.
source: Dual fluorescent RNA in situ hybridization of miR-488–3p and Cerox1 indicates the proximity of these non-coding RNAs within the N2A cell (Figure 5F) and that both Cerox1 and miR-488–3p are localised in the cytoplasm (Figures 1F and 5F).
evidence: The manuscript reports fluorescent in situ hybridization and fractionation results.

claim: CEROX1 transcripts are predominantly (94%) localised to ribosomes.
source: CEROX1 transcripts are predominantly (94%) localised to ribosomes (van Heesch et al., 2014)
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study reporting ribosome localization.

claim: Overexpression of miR-488-3p knocks down all 12 Cerox1-sensitive complex I subunit transcripts.
source: Results showed that miR-488–3p modulates these transcripts' levels, with overexpression leading to a significant downregulation of all 12 Cerox1-sensitive complex I transcripts (Figure 6A)
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR results from miRNA overexpression experiments.

claim: Inhibition of miR-488-3p leads to increased expression for 10 of 12 Cerox1-sensitive complex I transcripts, of which 4 were significantly increased.
source: whilst, conversely, miR-488–3p inhibition leads to increased expression for 10 of 12 transcripts, of which 4 (Ndufa2, Ndufb9, Ndufs4 and Ndufs1) were significantly increased (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR results from miRNA inhibition experiments.

claim: Mutations in the single predicted miR-488-3p MRE in Cerox1 abrogated the ability of miR-488-3p to destabilise Cerox1 transcript in a luciferase assay.
source: As expected for a bona fide MRE, these substitutions abrogated the ability of miR-488–3p to destabilise Cerox1 transcript in a luciferase assay (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript reports luciferase reporter assay results.

claim: Mutations in the miR-488-3p MRE abolished the ability of Cerox1 to elevate complex I transcript levels when overexpressed.
source: Importantly, these substitutions also abolished the ability of Cerox1, when overexpressed, to elevate complex I transcript levels (Figure 6E)
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR results from experiments with mutated Cerox1.

claim: Mutations in the miR-488-3p MRE abolished the ability of Cerox1 to enhance complex I enzymatic activity.
source: Importantly, these substitutions also abolished the ability of Cerox1, when overexpressed, to elevate complex I transcript levels (Figure 6E), and to enhance complex I enzymatic activity (Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results from experiments with mutated Cerox1.

claim: Direct physical interaction between Cerox1 and miR-488-3p was confirmed by pulling-down transcripts with biotinylated miR-488-3p.
source: Finally, direct physical interaction between Cerox1 and miR-488–3p was confirmed by pulling-down transcripts with biotinylated miR-488–3p (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript reports biotinylated miRNA pull-down assay results.

claim: 10 of 12 complex I transcripts tested were identified as direct targets of miR-488-3p binding by pull-down assay.
source: This experiment also identified 10 of 12 complex I transcripts tested as direct targets of miR-488–3p binding.
evidence: The manuscript reports biotinylated miRNA pull-down assay results.

claim: miR-488-3p directly regulates the transcript levels of at least 12 nuclear encoded mitochondrial complex I subunit genes (31% of all).
source: Consequently, our data demonstrates that miR-488–3p directly regulates the transcript levels of Cerox1 and at least 12 nuclear encoded mitochondrial complex I subunit genes (31% of all) and indirectly modulates complex I activity (Figure 6F) in N2A cells.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes multiple experimental results supporting this conclusion.

claim: Human CEROX1 is enriched in the cytoplasm of HEK293T cells.
source: Similar to mouse Cerox1, human CEROX1 is highly expressed in brain tissue, is otherwise ubiquitously expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and is enriched in the cytoplasm of human embryonic kidney (HEK293T) cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript reports cell fractionation results for human cells.

claim: CEROX1 occurs among the top 0.3% of all expressed lncRNAs in human tissues.
source: CEROX1 is expressed in human tissues at unusually high levels: it occurs among the top 0.3% of all expressed lncRNAs (Figure 7B)
evidence: The manuscript reports expression ranking from GTEx data.

claim: CEROX1 average expression is higher than 87.5% of all protein coding genes in human tissues.
source: CEROX1 is expressed in human tissues at unusually high levels: it occurs among the top 0.3% of all expressed lncRNAs (Figure 7B) and its average expression is higher than 87.5% of all protein coding genes (GTEx Consortium, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript reports expression comparison to protein-coding genes from GTEx data.

claim: CEROX1 expression is highest within brain tissues, particularly within the basal ganglia and cortex.
source: Its expression is highest within brain tissues, particularly within the basal ganglia and cortex (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript reports tissue-specific expression patterns from GTEx data.

claim: Complex I activity increased by 31% following CEROX1 overexpression in HEK293T cells.
source: Importantly, mitochondrial complexes' I and III activities increased significantly following CEROX1 overexpression in HEK293T cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results from human cell experiments.

claim: Complex III activity increased by 18% following CEROX1 overexpression in HEK293T cells.
source: Importantly, mitochondrial complexes' I and III activities increased significantly following CEROX1 overexpression in HEK293T cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results from human cell experiments.

claim: CEROX1 overexpression in HEK293T cells resulted in a 35% increase in basal respiration.
source: In addition to these observed increases in enzyme activity, basal respiration increased by 35%, ATP-linked respiration increase by 31% and maximum uncoupled respiration increased by 31% (p=0.02, p=0.04, p=0.01 respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 7E).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements with statistical significance.

claim: CEROX1 overexpression in HEK293T cells resulted in a 31% increase in ATP-linked respiration.
source: In addition to these observed increases in enzyme activity, basal respiration increased by 35%, ATP-linked respiration increase by 31% and maximum uncoupled respiration increased by 31% (p=0.02, p=0.04, p=0.01 respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 7E).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements with statistical significance.

claim: CEROX1 overexpression in HEK293T cells resulted in a 31% increase in maximum uncoupled respiration.
source: In addition to these observed increases in enzyme activity, basal respiration increased by 35%, ATP-linked respiration increase by 31% and maximum uncoupled respiration increased by 31% (p=0.02, p=0.04, p=0.01 respectively, 2-tailed Student's t-test; Figure 7E).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Reciprocal expression of mouse Cerox1 in human HEK293T cells or human CEROX1 in mouse N2A cells recapitulates the increase in complex I activity.
source: Strikingly, either reciprocal expression of mouse Cerox1 in human HEK293T cells or human CEROX1 in mouse N2A cells, recapitulates the previously observed increase in complex I activity (Figure 7F).
evidence: The manuscript reports enzyme activity assay results from cross-species experiments.

claim: The role of both Cerox1 and CEROX1 in modulating the activity of mitochondrial complex I has been conserved over 90 million years since the last common ancestor of mouse and human.
source: The role of both Cerox1 and CEROX1 in modulating the activity of mitochondrial complex I has thus been conserved over 90 million years since the last common ancestor of mouse and human.
evidence: The manuscript infers evolutionary conservation from the cross-species functional experiments.

claim: Cerox1 is the first evolutionarily conserved lncRNA demonstrated experimentally to regulate mitochondrial energy metabolism.
source: Cerox1 is the first evolutionarily conserved lncRNA to our knowledge that has been demonstrated experimentally to regulate mitochondrial energy metabolism.
evidence: The manuscript makes this claim based on the experimental results and literature review.

claim: Cerox1 post-transcriptionally regulates the levels of mitochondrial OXPHOS subunit transcripts and proteins by decoying for miRNAs, most particularly miR-488-3p.
source: Its principal location in N2A cells is in the cytoplasm (Figure 1F) where it post-transcriptionally regulates the levels of mitochondrial OXPHOS subunit transcripts and proteins by decoying for miRNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), most particularly miR-488–3p.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the mechanism based on multiple experimental results.

claim: miR-488-3p shares with Cerox1 an early eutherian origin and elevated expression in brain samples.
source: This microRNA shares with Cerox1 an early eutherian origin and elevated expression in brain samples (Landgraf et al., 2007)
evidence: The manuscript cites published work on miRNA evolution and expression.

claim: miR-488-3p was previously shown to alter mitochondrial dynamics in cancer cells.
source: This microRNA shares with Cerox1 an early eutherian origin and elevated expression in brain samples (Landgraf et al., 2007), and it previously was shown to alter mitochondrial dynamics in cancer cells (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published work on miR-488-3p function.

claim: The observed changes in catalytic activity are in line with the degree of change seen in diseases exhibiting mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: The observed changes in catalytic activity are in line with the degree of change seen in diseases exhibiting mitochondrial dysfunction (Schapira et al., 1990; Ritov et al., 2005; Andreazza et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript compares the magnitude of effects to published disease studies.

claim: Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases both feature pathophysiology associated with oxidative damage resulting from increased ROS production and a cellular energy deficit associated with decreased complex I and IV activities (a reduction of 30% and 40%, respectively).
source: Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases both feature pathophysiology associated with oxidative damage resulting from increased ROS production and a cellular energy deficit associated with decreased complex I and IV activities (a reduction of 30% and 40%, respectively) (Schapira et al., 1990; Keeney et al., 2006; Canevari et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies on mitochondrial dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: A 20% increase in complex I activity protects mouse midbrain dopaminergic neurons against MPP+, a complex I inhibitor and a chemical model of Parkinson's disease.
source: Currently no effective treatments exist that help to restore mitochondrial function despite demonstration that a 20% increase in complex I activity protects mouse midbrain dopaminergic neurons against MPP+, a complex I inhibitor and a chemical model of Parkinson's disease (Alvarez-Fischer et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study demonstrating neuroprotection from increased complex I activity.

claim: The highest expression of CEROX1 occurs primarily in the basal ganglia.
